title: Mental illness training key, inquest told; Man died after he was arrested Jury deliberates recommendations: [ONT Edition]
article: Continuing education for police officers, court officers and physicians who work with the mentally ill on the symptoms of excited delirium is one recommendation being considered at the inquest into the death of Nicholas Blentzas.
The jury began its deliberations yesterday after hearing evidence from 21 witnesses since the inquest began earlier this month.
Blentzas, who died while being arrested on June 22, 2002, suffered from an ongoing and degenerative mental illness.
The 24-year-old had been prescribed lithium by his doctor but had stopped taking it sometime before his arrest.

On the night he died, neighbours called police because Blentzas was trying to break into his own apartment with a fire extinguisher. Police officers found him in front of his apartment door, sweating and without his shirt, acting strangely. They persuaded him to go to the hospital with them.

But once he was out of the building's elevator, he bolted from police. Officers used pepper spray to try to subdue him, but it didn't work. Eventually, they wrestled him to the ground and handcuffed him. An ambulance was called, but Blentzas died before it arrived.
The Special Investigations Unit looked into the case and found there had been no wrongdoing by police. But as is the case when someone dies in police custody, a mandatory inquest was called.

Now the jury begins its deliberations with a list of proposed recommendations that David Carruthers, counsel for the coroner's office, hopes will help prevent similar deaths. The jury may accept or reject the recommendations or prepare new ones. It also must determine the cause and nature of Blentzas's death.
Carruthers stated in his final arguments that Blentzas died of "excited delirium due to acute exacerbation of a psychiatric illness." He urged jurors to give the man's death some meaning.
"You will be able through this process to speak for the dead to protect the living," Carruthers told the jury. "This inquest should be and can be a part of Nicholas Blentzas's legacy."

Toronto's police chief and the police services board continue to ensure recruits are taught the signs and symptoms of excited delirium and the risks associated with physically restraining someone suffering from it.
Police and court officers continue receiving a yearly refresher during their pepper-spray training on the signs and symptoms of excited delirium and its risks.

The Ontario Police College continue ensuring recruits are taught about excited delirium and its risks, and that the college continue to make sure trainees experience being physically restrained in the prone position.

The police college, the police chief and the Toronto Police Services Board think about including the facts of Blentzas's death in a role-playing exercise or case study to train officers on excited delirium.
The health ministry consider increasing funding to hospitals and psychiatric care facilities for more beds for patients who are there on a 72-hour assessment.
Nicholas Blentzas was much more than his mental illness, said Jean Buie, the lawyer representing his family. "They hope his death can achieve some meaning through your work," she told the jury.
